about: Spoken-register guidance for voice agents, per call language and business type. AI-drafted 10 Oct 2026 and expanded 11 Oct 2026 (founder decisions 3, 10 Oct, and the 11 Oct spoken-style rules). EVERY entry here is needs_native_review except prompt_examples (founder approved 14 Oct 2026, see its note): the founder reviews them on the admin screen Ops > Spoken style, whose published edits are stored in the database and layered over this file (calevate_shared.spoken_style.install_published). What each part is for: register is the one-line description of how the language is spoken; word_swaps pairs a formal or written form (left) with what people actually say (right), and the ones named in prompt_swaps go into every agent's prompt in that language, while the whole list guides the script writer, the test callers and the test checks; fillers are the spoken tags and light fillers people use; number_rules and punctuation say how numbers and sentences are written for a voice; examples are example exchanges per business type that show HOW to speak, never facts (no price, time, address or stock level, so an agent cannot repeat a made-up fact); openings are a starter's greeting. Register sources for te-IN: Telugu has a literary register (grandhika) and a spoken standard (vyavaharika, the sishta vyavaharika of educated everyday speech), the latter championed by Gidugu Venkata Ramamurthy (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gidugu_Venkata_Ramamurthy; https://www.deccanchronicle.com/lifestyle/culture-and-society/telugu-language-day-commemorates-gidugu-revolutionary-behind-simple-telugu-usage-1983163). Telugu-English code-mixing ('Tenglish') is extensively used in Hyderabad (Dutta and Rajeswari, Texas Linguistics Forum 2015, https://asol.ling.utexas.edu/salsa/proceedings/2015/Dutta.pdf); Standard and Telangana Telugu differences and code-mixing in speech are studied in Sravani, Kameswari and Mamidi 2021 (https://aclanthology.org/2021.calcs-1.1). Voice facts (Cartesia, read 11 Oct 2026): sonic-3.6 lists Telugu (te); it varies pacing and intonation to the transcript without SSML, pause length adapts to the sentence, and disfluencies such as 'uhm' give a thinking pace (https://docs.cartesia.ai/build-with-cartesia/tts-models/latest); full, punctuated sentences ending in . ? or ! give the best pacing (https://docs.cartesia.ai/build-with-cartesia/sonic-3-5/prompting-tips). Code-switching is documented only for Hindi written in Latin script; Telugu-English mixing is UNVERIFIED in the vendor docs and confirmed only by the founder's ear test ("whole chilli", "call", "kg" spoken naturally). The number style (prices, quantities and times in English words as shop people say them) is the founder's decision of 11 Oct 2026; Cartesia's own guidance would let the model normalise digits, which the founder's ear test overrode for Telugu calls.

te-IN.register: Everyday spoken Telugu (vyavaharika, never grandhika or bookish), neutral for both Telangana and Andhra, in Telugu script; the English words people use stay in English letters (order, price, delivery, call, kg). అండి and గారు by situation, not in every sentence.

fillers.use: Acknowledging what the caller said or asked for.
Short yes, or showing you are listening.
Mild surprise or 'is that so?' after news from the caller.
A tag asking for agreement: '..., కదా?'
A casual 'what?', as in 'ఏంటి problem?'
Before checking something or looking it up.
'I mean' or 'that is', before rephrasing.
Okay, between steps.
A polite yes.
'Sure, will do' to a request.
'Go ahead, tell me' when the caller starts.
'Good' when the caller agrees to a next step.
Sympathy when the caller has a problem: 'అయ్యో, sorry అండి.'
Reassuring after the caller apologises or declines.

number_rules.text: Prices in English words the way shop people say them: 120 rupees is "one twenty rupees", 250 is "two fifty rupees", 1,500 is "fifteen hundred rupees". Never write the rupee sign or digits.
Big amounts as people say them: "seventy lakhs", "one point two crores".
Quantities and units in English: "one kg", "half kg", "two litres", "five hundred grams", "two BHK", "twelve hundred square feet".
Times in English: "five o'clock", "ten thirty". The part of the day can stay Telugu: "పొద్దున ten o'clock", "సాయంత్రం five thirty".
రేపు, ఎల్లుండి and ఈరోజు stay Telugu; weekdays and dates are English: "Monday", "the twelfth".
Phone numbers, OTPs and codes one digit at a time in English: "nine eight four nine".
Small everyday counts can stay Telugu (రెండు నిమిషాలు, ఒక్క సెకండ్); a price, a quantity or a time is said in English.

punctuation.text: Short sentences, one idea each. Split a long sentence into two.
A comma where you would take a breath: "సరే అండి, ఒక్క నిమిషం."
A question mark on every question and a full stop at the end of every other sentence.
No dashes, slashes, brackets, ellipses, quotation marks, bullets or emoji: the voice reads them or stumbles on them.
No dotted abbreviations: "Dr Ravi", never "Dr. Ravi"; say "rupees", never "Rs".
English words in English letters (delivery, not డెలివరీ) and Telugu words in Telugu script.
Two choices as two short questions, "whole chilli కావాలా, powder కావాలా?", rather than a list joined with లేదా.

en-IN.register: Simple, warm Indian English as people speak on the phone. Sir or madam once, not every line. Mix in Hindi or Telugu words if the caller does.

clinic: I want to see the doctor. Can I get an appointment?

real_estate: Do you have 2 BHK flats in the project?

local_services: Is there a slot for a haircut tomorrow?

automobile: I need my bike serviced. When can I bring it?
